title: Height does not impair the hydraulic system of the tallest tropical Dipterocarp trees.
data_url: https://doi.org/10.5285/6ecfd160-4740-491e-a8b3-8cbb3a4c8701 (trait table, NERC EIDC) and https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.d51c5b0j4 (growth data + R code, Dryad)

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed the real trait table from the NERC Environmental Information Data Centre (EIDC): borneo_tree_traits_2022.csv, 72 KB zip, 156 KB unzipped, 389 rows x 29 columns, 38 unique tree identifiers, 5 dipterocarp species, tree height 7.7-71.0 m. Counted non-null values per trait column (68 to 299), 3 exactly duplicated rows, and per-species tree counts (6 to 10 trees each). Also read the complete Dryad README (every column name and unit for both growth spreadsheets) and the Dryad file listing with sizes from the Dryad application programming interface (API).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The Dryad files themselves (dendrometerData.xlsx 142 KB, traitsSummaryTable.xlsx 16 KB, analysis.r 17 KB) could not be opened: Dryad serves an Anubis proof-of-work bot challenge, so both the API and the direct file links return 401/403 to any non-browser client. The claim of '42 trees' with dendrometer growth, and the daily-growth-rate row count, therefore rest on the Dryad README description only, not on the file. The Science full text is paywalled and absent from PubMed Central, so methods detail comes from the two data READMEs.
verified.note: Licences are permissive: CC0 1.0 on Dryad, UK Open Government Licence on EIDC. The block is bot protection, not an access restriction.

a1_downloadable.note: The main trait table downloaded in one step from EIDC with no login (Open Government Licence). The Dryad half (growth time series) is public and CC0 but blocked to scripts by an Anubis proof-of-work challenge; a human with a browser can get it.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Candidate targets are already columns of measured values: p50branch and p88branch (the water tension at which a branch loses 50% or 88% of its water-transport capacity), TLP (leaf turgor loss point), psiMD (midday water potential). No construction needed.

a3_inputs_present.note: Predictors are present as numbers in the same file: treeHeight, sampleHeight, sampleDiameter, distanceFromTip, vesselDiameter, vesselDensity, woodDensity, leaf mass per area. No identifier lookups required.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are given for every variable in both READMEs (megapascals for pressures, micrometres for vessel diameter, grams per square metre for leaf mass per area, micrometres per day for growth) and are internally consistent.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAILS. 389 measurement rows total, far below the ~1,500 threshold, and they are nested inside only 38 trees and 5 species. The best complete-case table for a trait-prediction task is 210 rows (wood anatomy plus branch P50) across 34 trees, or 64 rows if a full multi-trait feature set is required. Counted in the file.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Noted in passing after A5 failed: 156 KB unzipped, trivially laptop-sized.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Noted in passing after A5 failed. The EIDC record states '25 traits' and '12 measurement points per tree' for 38 trees; the file holds 21 trait columns and 4 to 17 rows per tree (median 10). Dryad separately reports 42 trees for the growth data versus 38 here. Minor, but unresolved.

a8_label_provenance.note: Noted in passing after A5 failed. All candidate labels trace to physical measurements made in a 2022 field campaign (pressure chamber, air-injection embolism curves, light-microscope vessel counts); none is another model's output. One caveat: droughtGrowthReduction in the Dryad file is defined as 100*GR_enso/GR_reference, so its two component columns must never be used as features.

honest_claim_h3: Not applicable: with 38 trees and 5 species from one 48-hectare reserve, any model could only claim 'describes how hydraulic traits vary with height among these 38 Bornean dipterocarps', which is what the paper's own mixed-effects regression already states with proper uncertainty.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use tree height and wood vessel anatomy to predict how much drought tension a branch can take before its water pipes fail.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example is one sampling point on one tree (trunk base, trunk top, or a branch in the lower, middle or upper crown), described by tree height, sample height, branch diameter, distance from the twig tip, mean xylem vessel diameter and vessel density. I verified 389 such rows in the file, but only 210 have both the wood anatomy and the target measured, spread over 34 trees.
plain_idea.predict: The output is P50 (the xylem water pressure, in megapascals, at which a branch loses half its capacity to move water). The true value comes from air-injection vulnerability curves measured on freshly cut branches in a field laboratory in Sabah, Borneo, during 2022.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Forest-carbon and vegetation models need a rule for how tall trees adjust their plumbing, because half of a forest's above-ground carbon sits in a few giants. Even a failed model would show how much of this trait variation height and anatomy cannot explain.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: predict branch embolism resistance (P50) or leaf turgor loss point from tree height plus xylem vessel anatomy, with leave-one-species-out validation. The data is beautifully documented and permissively licensed, but at 389 rows nested in 38 trees and 5 species it is a mixed-effects regression dataset, not a machine-learning dataset; the paper already analyses it that way. The only honest machine-learning use would be as one small site inside a much larger pooled compilation (for example the TRY plant trait database or the Xylem Functional Traits database), which is a different project with a different primary dataset.

effort.compute_note: Measured, not estimated: the 72 KB zip downloaded in under a second and pandas read the 389-row CSV instantly. Any model on this table runs in seconds on a laptop CPU.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count unique values in the 'tree' column of borneo_tree_traits_2022.csv. The answer is 38, with 5 species, which kills the project in one line of code.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A5 on sample size, verified in the downloaded file: 389 trait measurements nested in only 38 trees and 5 species (210 rows for the most complete feature-label combination), against a ~1,500-row threshold. The independent unit is the tree, and the paper's question is about a tree-level variable (height), so the row count is pseudo-replication, exactly the 'A5 in disguise' failure mode. Three secondary strikes: the Dryad growth data is unopenable by script because of a proof-of-work bot challenge, so its 42-tree claim is unverified; missingness is severe (several traits measured on only 68 to 78 rows); and the EIDC metadata's '12 measurement points per tree' does not match the file's 4 to 17. The data is genuinely high quality and permissively licensed, it is simply the wrong size and shape for machine learning.
